span.label: critique
span.quote: At the same time, the work demonstrates some potential pitfalls and limits of this approach to philosophy.

span.label: philosophical accounts of evidence
span.quote: The first part of the book consists of five chapters which deal with philosophical problems surrounding the notion of evidence.

span.label: review
span.quote: The book, or a selection of essays from it, could profitably be used as course material for an advanced seminar in the philosophy of science.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Explanatory adequacy is context-dependent because what it takes to make something understandable varies with the audience's interests and background knowledge, so the same act explains for one hearer and not another
span.quote: As Achinstein notes, this makes explanation a context-dependent matter, given that what exactly has to be done to make something understandable to someone may depend on the interests and background knowledge of the person seeking understanding.

span.label: Usage data does not settle which analysis of a concept is right, so the choice between rival definitions has to be made on other grounds.
span.quote: Further, in philosophy it is rarely the case that linguistic intuitions point to precisely one analysis of a given concept. We almost always have to arbitrate between different concept explications on the basis of something other than data about language use

span.label: The counterexample that motivates the alternative definition only bites under one of the word's two ordinary uses, and dissolves under the other.
span.quote: while we often use the word ‘evidence’ in a categorical sense—as when we say that something is (or is not) evidence for something else—we also use it in a graded sense, when we say that something is strong (or weak) evidence for something else. And although in the above lottery case it may sound strange to say that the information that 99 of 100 tickets have been given to Mary and the remaining ticket has been given to John is evidence (in the categorical sense) for John’s winning the lottery, perhaps it is not so 123 Evidence, Explanation, and Realism 599 strange to say that to an exceedingly low degree it is evidence for John’s winning the lottery, whereas it is evidence for Mary’s winning the lottery to a very high degree

span.label: The book reprints a theory the reviewer says is no longer influential, without answering the criticisms that made it so.
span.quote: It is fair to say that Achinstein’s work on explanation is no longer influential, due to a large extent to criticisms leveled against it. It would have been a welcome addition to this collection of essays if Achinstein had, perhaps in an appendix to some of the papers, indicated why he believes the theory still stands

span.label: theoretical virtues
span.quote: Carnap famously proposed that such arbitration should take place on the basis of the so-called theoretical virtues, such as simplicity and fruitfulness

span.label: evidence - BAYESIAN: E is evidence for H exactly when H becomes more probable given E; purely formal, and the account the rest of the argument is aimed at
span.quote: Bayesians have a purely formal and entirely straightforward conception of evidence: E is evidence for a hypothesis H if, and only if, the probability of H conditional on E is greater than the unconditional probability of H

span.label: evidence - ACHINSTEIN'S, SPLIT IN TWO: the hypothesis must be probable given the evidence, not merely more probable, AND there must be an explanatory connection - probable for POTENTIAL evidence, actually existing for VERIDICAL evidence
span.quote: he first distinguishes between two different notions of evidence—potential and veridical evidence—and then goes on to define them in ways that draw not only on probability theory (as does the Bayesian definition) but also on the notion of explanation. To solve the lottery problem, Achinstein requires that for something to count as evidence for something else, the latter must be probable given the former, not (necessarily) more probable. But that is still not enough. That Jim will not get pregnant is quite probable given the fact that he takes the pill, yet his taking the pill is not evidence of his not getting pregnant. To avoid this kind of problem, Achinstein adds as a necessary condition to his definition that there be an explanatory connection between the putative evidence and the hypothesis—or rather, for potential evidence, it has to be probable that there is such a connection; for veridical evidence, it has to actually exist

span.label: evidence - THE REVIEWER'S PURELY PROBABILISTIC DEFINITION: probable given E and more probable than unconditionally, which he argues covers every case the explanatory clause was added for
span.quote: For instance, the purely probabilistic definition: E is evidence for H if and only if both H is probable given E and H is more probable given E than it is unconditionally

span.label: evidence - CATEGORICAL vs GRADED: the same word is used both for a yes-or-no relation and for a matter of degree, and which one is meant decides whether the lottery case is a problem at all
span.quote: while we often use the word ‘evidence’ in a categorical sense—as when we say that something is (or is not) evidence for something else—we also use it in a graded sense, when we say that something is strong (or weak) evidence for something else

span.label: contradicts → Peter Achinstein's definition of potential and veridical evidence
span.quote: I am not convinced that Achinstein’s proposal offers the simplest way to make sense of the relevant linguistic data.

span.label: potential evidence —is-a→ evidence
span.quote: he first distinguishes between two different notions of evidence—potential and veridical evidence

span.label: veridical evidence —is-a→ evidence
span.quote: he first distinguishes between two different notions of evidence—potential and veridical evidence—and then goes on to define them

span.label: potential evidence —distinct-from→ veridical evidence
span.quote: for potential evidence, it has to be probable that there is such a connection; for veridical evidence, it has to actually exist

span.label: Achinstein rejects the Bayesian probability-raising conception of evidence because in a 100-ticket lottery where Mary holds 99 tickets, the Bayesian account counts the news that John received a ticket as evidence that John will win, when the same information is really evidence that Mary will win.
span.quote: But, if it is evidence for anything, the said information is evidence that Mary will win the lottery—which would seem to constitute evidence against John’s winning.

span.label: Achinstein's own account replaces probability-raising with a high-probability requirement: the hypothesis must be probable given the putative evidence, not merely more probable than before.
span.quote: To solve the lottery problem, Achinstein requires that for something to count as evidence for something else, the latter must be probable given the former, not (necessarily) more probable.

span.label: Achinstein additionally requires an explanatory connection between evidence and hypothesis, which need only be probable for potential evidence but must actually obtain for veridical evidence.
span.quote: To avoid this kind of problem, Achinstein adds as a necessary condition to his definition that there be an explanatory connection between the putative evidence and the hypothesis—or rather, for potential evidence, it has to be probable that there is such a connection; for veridical evidence, it has to actually exist.

span.label: Douven argues that a simpler purely probabilistic definition, requiring both that the hypothesis be probable given the evidence and that the evidence raise its probability, already disposes of Achinstein's lottery case and his pill/pregnancy case without invoking explanation.
span.quote: Obviously, it solves the lottery problem, and it also handles perfectly the case of Jim’s likelihood of pregnancy: It is probable that Jim will not get pregnant given that he takes the pill, but this is no more probable than that Jim will not get pregnant, regardless of whether he takes the pill.

span.label: Douven rejects Achinstein's medication counterexample by arguing the probability-lowering information can be re-described as a good reason to believe rather than as evidence, since not every good reason to believe something is evidence for it.
span.quote: Alternatively, you could grant that that piece of information is not evidence but still a good reason to believe the person’s symptoms will be relieved—and that that might fuel the intuition that it is evidence.

span.label: Achinstein argues that Bayesian and rival philosophical accounts of evidence are too weak to be used in science and wrongly treat evidential status as knowable a priori, whereas two historical case studies show it can be an empirical matter.
span.quote: Not only are the notions of evidence offered by these accounts too weak to be of any use in science, they are meant to apply on a priori grounds, while—as Achinstein argues with two case studies—it is, or at any rate can be, rather an empirical matter whether a given datum is evidence for a given theory.

span.label: Because Achinstein makes the act of explaining central, whether someone explained something depends on that person's intention, so uttering words that in fact produce understanding without the intention to do so is not explaining.
span.quote: Moreover, because the act of explanation is central to Achinstein’s theory, a person’s intentions matter in regard to whether or not he or she explained something; if he or she had no intention of making something understandable to someone, then he or she did not explain the thing—even if he or she uttered words that, as a matter of fact, made the thing understandable to the persons in his or her audience.

span.label: Douven's verdict is that Achinstein's theory of explanation has lost its influence, largely because of the criticisms directed at it, and that the volume should have said why Achinstein still holds it.
span.quote: It is fair to say that Achinstein’s work on explanation is no longer influential, due to a large extent to criticisms leveled against it.

span.label: Douven judges that Achinstein's study of Perrin's Brownian-motion work is the strongest available defence of scientific realism, because antirealists who resist it end up in the position of a global external-world skeptic.
span.quote: Antirealists may be able to hold their position in the face of Perrin’s findings, but in doing so, they will come to resemble the philosophical skeptic who implores us to remain agnostic about the existence of an external world in general (and not just the unobservable part of the world).

span.label: Bayesian conception of evidence
span.quote: Bayesians have a purely formal and entirely straightforward conception of evidence: E is evidence for a hypothesis H if, and only if, the probability of H conditional on E is greater than the unconditional probability of H.

span.label: potential evidence vs. veridical evidence
span.quote: Or rather, he first distinguishes between two different notions of evidence—potential and veridical evidence—and then goes on to define them in ways that draw not only on probability theory (as does the Bayesian definition) but also on the notion of explanation.

span.label: purely probabilistic definition of evidence (Douven's alternative)
span.term: purely probabilistic definition of evidence (Douven's alternative)
span.quote: E is evidence for H if and only if both H is probable given E and H is more probable given E than it is unconditionally.

span.label: explanation (as making understandable to someone)
span.quote: Specifically, to explain something is to make that thing understandable to someone.

span.label: scientific realism
span.quote: Scientific realists believe that science is by and large successful in charting the unobservable part of the world.

span.label: underdetermination
span.quote: Antirealists are typically motivated by the problem of underdetermination, that is, the problem that even if the data favor precisely one of the theories on the table (which need not be the case), there will be many other theories, possibly not (yet) conceived, that receive or would receive equal or perhaps even stronger support from the data.

span.label: theoretical virtues
span.quote: Carnap famously proposed that such arbitration should take place on the basis of the so-called theoretical virtues, such as simplicity and fruitfulness.
